new_statements.quote: 南方言と同様に、声の高低（ピッチ）変化によるアクセント（高低アクセント）を認める。どの単語（句）においてもアクセントの位置やパターンは一定で、非弁別的である（津曲 1983、Tsumagari 2009）。さらに語の後ろから 2 番目のモーラ（それが副モーラの場合は、その前の主モーラ）が高く発音され、これをアクセントの峰とする（Tsumagari 2009: 3–4）。2 モーラから成り第一モーラが高くなる語以外は、語の最初から二番目のモーラからアクセントの峰までが高く発音される（ibid.）。この原則は、おおむね北方言にも適用できる。しかし、今日の北方言では同一母音の連続（長母音）に強さアクセントを置く傾向がある。
new_statements.translation: As in the southern dialect, an accent realised by change in voice pitch (a pitch accent) is recognised. In every word (or phrase) the position and pattern of the accent are constant and non-distinctive (Tsumagari 1983, Tsumagari 2009). Further, the second mora from the end of the word (or, if that is a secondary mora, the main mora before it) is pronounced high, and this is taken as the accent peak (Tsumagari 2009: 3–4). Except in words of two moras whose first mora is high, everything from the second mora of the word up to the accent peak is pronounced high (ibid.). This principle can, on the whole, be applied to the northern dialect as well. However, in the northern dialect today there is a tendency to place a stress accent on sequences of identical vowels (long vowels). [p. 58]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Uilta with an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements; this work supplies the placement (non-contrastive pitch accent, peak on the penultimate mora, or the preceding main mora when the penult is a secondary mora, citing Tsumagari 1983 and 2009 for the southern dialect and extending it to the northern dialect) plus the modern northern-dialect stress-on-long-vowel tendency. Nothing in the catalog contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive pitch accent whose position is fixed: the high peak is on the penultimate mora of the word; if that mora is a secondary mora (second half of a long vowel/diphthong, or a coda consonant), the peak shifts to the preceding main mora (i.e. the syllable-initial CV). From the second mora of the word up to the peak the pitch is high (a plateau); words of two moras with a high first mora are the exception. This is Tsumagari's (1983, 2009) analysis of the southern dialect, which Yamada says applies on the whole to the northern dialect. In addition, present-day northern-dialect speakers tend to put a Russian-style stress accent on long vowels (identical-vowel sequences), e.g. ok|soo [ɑksɔ́ː] 'reindeer sledge', bo|boo|nik|ka [bɑbɔ́ːniqqɑ] 'hood', joo|do|pu [jɔ́ːdɑpu], o|juu|kam|ba [ɑjúːkɑmbɑ] 'a little', see|to|si|či [ʃɛ́ːtɑʃitʃi] (p. 58), with an adjacent /o/ reduced to [ɑ] as in Russian; the conclusion (p. 66) says the accent features show strong Russian influence, and the English summary (p. 70) puts it as 'ND speakers tend to pronounce with the stress on diphthongs'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned. The description is of one peak per word plus a high plateau from the second mora to the peak.
new_statements.exceptions: Two-mora words whose first mora is high (peak on the first mora). In the modern northern dialect the stress-accent tendency on long vowels (Russian contact) overrides the mora-counting pattern in narrative speech; when speakers are asked to repeat, /o/ is again [o] (p. 58). Yamada notes (p. 66) that because the southern dialect was described in the early 20th century and the northern in the 1990s-2010s, the differences may be language change under Russian contact rather than pure dialect differences.
new_statements.identity_note: Yamada 2017 describes the northern dialect of Uilta (Val, northern Sakhalin), contrasting it with the southern dialect (Poronaisk); the pitch accent rule she quotes is Tsumagari's analysis of the southern dialect, which she says applies on the whole to the northern dialect too. The stress-on-long-vowels tendency is specific to present-day northern-dialect speakers.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the Tsumagari 2009 PDF we hold/txt at sec. 2.4 (p.3) and sec. 2.6 (pp.3-4). (2) The classification rests on a 2009 grammar sketch, but by the language's principal specialist summarising his own dedicated 1983 accent study; a repository and catalogue search (TUFS, HUSCAP via CiNii/IRDB, CiNii 97 hits, Cambridge Core/JIPA, Crossref) found no instrumental or competing phonological analysis. (3) Three Glottolog-listed or related works were downloaded openly and read: Yamada 2017 repeats the identical penultimate-mora pitch accent rule for the Northern dialect (refines: Russian-influenced tendency to stress long vowels); Novikova & Sem 1997 state word stress is 'unclear, not experimentally studied'; Petrova 1967 has no stress section. Nothing contradicts the weight-sensitive right-edge coding (peak on final syllable if CVV/CVC, else penult; non-phonemic pitch accent).

tone.says: Per Yamada 2017: 53 ('大部分は池上(1955, 1971, 1997a, 2001b)、津曲(1988)、Tsumagari(1985, 2009)らが記述している南方言の特徴と共通する') it is one of the primary descriptions of Southern-Uilta phonology; a Kenkyusha 'Sekai gengo gaisetsu' sketch normally has an accent paragraph, and this would be the earliest first-hand remark on Orok accent (three decades before Tsumagari 1983) if it has one. Basis: work type and secondary characterisation only.
